/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.headline: Revealed: French police used UK-funded 4x4 vehicles to charge student protesters
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.excerpt: French police have used 4x4 vehicles paid for by British taxpayers to charge at student protesters during the school protests that have swept the country. The French government has confirmed that an investigation has been launched into why the cars, funded by the UK government specifically to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel, were used during a protest involving school students in Dunkirk. School protests have been taking place across France for a third week with an estimated 160,000 people involved, with protesters raising concerns about crumbling schools and teacher shortages. Demonstrators have criticised policing tactics after teargas was fired at protesters in two areas. The incident involving the UK-funded 4x4, a land cruiser known as Masstech VEZI (Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention), was reported by French media outlet BFM TV on 10 October. The report included footage of the VEZI driving at speed, reversing then driving forwards again with a bin caught under a front wheel being dragged along. Students can be heard screaming as they scatter from the path of the vehicle. According to reports, a 14-year-old girl was injured by the vehicle and was taken to hospital, sustaining a haematoma. She was later discharged from hospital. She is now recovering, but she told reporters that what happened to her was “unacceptable”.
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.trail: French government investigating why cars funded by UK to prevent asylum seekers crossing Channel were used in school protests

/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.headline: France’s class action: inside the 16 October Guardian Weekly
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.excerpt: France has been rocked by huge youth protests in recent weeks over the state of high school education, bringing tens of thousands of people on to the streets. The movement began with outrage over shoddy school conditions in a Paris banlieue, but has spread across the country as pupils voice their anger about a system they say is failing them. For this week’s big story, Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis hears from protesters who feel abandoned by the French state. Angelique also looks at the evidence on students’ complaints of dilapidated buildings, teacher shortages, inequality and low investment. Then, Alexander Hurst says fixing the broken education system should be just the start for an aloof political class if it is to finally pay attention to a generation who feel neglected. /world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.trail: What drove student protests? Plus: Duran Duran’s extraordinary world

/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.headline: France’s students are angry about more than crumbling classrooms and missing teachers
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.excerpt: Say what you will about France’s high schools, they still produce world-class slogan writers. Here’s a brief selection spotted during three weeks of blockades and marches over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings: “Pas d’avenir, pas de calme” (No future, no calm). “Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain” (Graduates today, insecure tomorrow). “Vous détruisez notre futur, on bloque votre présent” (You destroy our future, we block your present). A couple more: “Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs” (Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”). “On n’est pas mal éduqués, on n’est pas écoutés” (We’re not badly brought up, we’re just not being listened to). Spot the common theme? The protests, which continued this week with more than 160,000 on the streets on Tuesday, might be over very material problems – but beneath them there clearly lies an altogether more existential worry. This generation fears its future will be one of diminishing prospects, poorly paid, unstable jobs, unaffordable living costs and steadily decaying public infrastructure – the end, in short, of the basic socioeconomic security their parents, mostly, enjoyed. That was the central theme of a 30-second Instagram post I recorded last week with the Guardian’s social media team and that, at time of writing, had been watched almost 540,000 times – with young people in France the largest single group of viewers.
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.trail: Beneath a wave of school protests in France lies an altogether more existential worry: the future prospects of an entire generation

/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.headline: At least 160,000 people take to streets in third week of French school protests
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.excerpt: More than 160,000 schoolchildren, students and trade unionists have marched in cities across France as protests over high school education continued into a third week and many demonstrators denounced policing tactics. Riot police fired teargas at the end of Tuesday’s marches in Nantes and near the Montparnasse area of Paris, but most of the demonstrations over teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling school buildings held in cities including Lyon, Lille and Marseille were peaceful. The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg joined an early morning protest outside the Lycée Paul Éluard in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. “Young people are not being included in the conversation,” said Thunberg, 23, who became famous as a teenager through school strikes demanding action on the climate crisis. As lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect pupils after accusations of police brutality, Thunberg said: “Our future is being stolen from us and, as we have seen here, schools are not getting the investment they need.” Students outside the high school said Thunberg had encouraged them to continue with peaceful demonstrations. The protests – backed by trade unionists, some teachers and radical leftwing opposition politicians – have shaken a government caught between calls for urgent public investment and pressure to reduce France’s ballooning deficit and debt.
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.trail: Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joins teenagers calling for investment to fix teacher shortages and crumbling schools

/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.headline: France’s dilemma: protesters demand spending as markets require fiscal restraint
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.excerpt: Eight years have passed since rising fuel prices brought the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) demonstrators to the streets of France, prompting the first big crisis of Emmanuel Macron’s time in the Élysée Palace. As the French president contemplates his exit next year, turmoil has again gripped the streets in the form of student protests, but this time the financial markets are unhappy too. Investors are concerned about the government’s failure to bring spending under control and end a long period of “fiscal incontinence”. Financial markets are unnerved by similar trends in the UK, the US and more recently Italy, causing jitters in global bond markets. But it’s France that has become the biggest worry, hemmed in by debts across the public and private sectors, limiting their scope to dig the country out of a deepening hole. France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% for the UK respectively. In Britain, the chancellor, John Healey, is on course to reduce the budget deficit this year and in 2027. His French counterpart, Roland Lescure, has promised to follow suit after a rise to 5.4% this year, but has yet to say how. ‘I am panicking’ One victim of the uncertainty is business investment. A survey by Medef, France’s largest employer federation, showed 82% of firms were pessimistic about the impact of the next government’s economic policy.
/world/2026/oct/17/protests-france-high-.trail: Waves of protests expose debt crisis faced by French government, but political wrangling is stalling an escape plan. Is there a way out?

/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.headline: Unpolished, anti-Bibi, but evasive on peace: who is the Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot?
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.excerpt: He has been called the man who is everything the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, is not. Gadi Eisenkot, a former general and the main opposition candidate in Israel’s elections this month, is unpolished where Netanyahu is slick. To Israelis he is both menschy (decent) and schlumpy (unkempt), his crumpled appearance contrasting with Netanyahu’s hair rinse, makeup and obsessive need to control his media depiction. In the Israeli commentator Anshel Pfeffer’s framing, he is the anti-Bibi among a roster of wanna-Bibis. And in an era of Israeli politics that has been defined by betrayals, dirty tricks and public and private smears, Eisenkot’s brand is rectitude. He only entered politics four years ago, and the name of his party – Yashar – means “straight” or “honest”. But on key issues, an Israel under Eisenkot may not look very different, as he has been non-committal on crucial issues – including the two-state solution and Israeli settlement of the occupied West Bank. “He’s not sleek. He’s not corrupt. I think he’s going to be looking more inwards than outwards. Because he’s a military guy, he’s interested in calming the waters,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst for the International Crisis Group. “[But] he’s hedging a lot.” For many voters, Eisenkot’s appeal is less about ideology than the vibe around him. Key to his appeal, said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political analyst, is his “very modest background”.
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.trail: The ‘menschy’ former general contrasts with the current PM when it comes to style and character – yet on key policy points retains a studied ambiguity

/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.headline: New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.excerpt: The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners. The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person. Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation. The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government. The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it. Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement. The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.trail: Global human rights commitments adopted by government extend reach to enablers of unlawful activity

/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.headline: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.excerpt: Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel. The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza. The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after demonstrators climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial, having Palestine Action placards, making a Nazi salute and assaulting police as officers made arrests. Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.trail: Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful

/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.headline: ‘Self-imposed irrelevance’: why the EU is failing to act on growing public criticism of Israel
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.excerpt: When the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not. Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect. A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government. A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel. Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%. Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion.
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.trail: While Israel’s actions against Palestinians intensify public anger, the bloc remains paralysed along familiar fault lines

/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.headline: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.excerpt: Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving the region, with only seven to remain in the building. Among those leaving is the consul general, Helen Winterton. The change was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those who aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two-state solution as the best means of ending the Israel-Palestine conflict. Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign. There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics. Israel had ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed.
/world/2026/oct/17/israeli-settlers-atta.trail: UK and Israel back away from full diplomatic confrontation, though British presence in Palestine will be much reduced

/politics/2026/oct/17/reform-candidate-f.headline: Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, says equalities minister
/politics/2026/oct/17/reform-candidate-f.excerpt: Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, the equalities minister has said, as she warned that young men were being sucked into violent misogyny by the “cesspit” of social media. Bridget Phillipson said she was increasingly worried about how commonplace misogyny and racism had become, fuelled by online interactions and statements by politicians she said would not have been acceptable a few years ago. She accused senior MPs from Reform and the Conservatives of having made racist statements in recent years, and accused the police of not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast, she said: “I worry that we are at kind of a ground zero in terms of attitudes around violence against women and girls. Things that not very long ago felt totally unacceptable are becoming normal. I think we’re seeing that in terms of attitudes towards women, and I think we see that in terms of attitudes around racism.” She accused the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, and Reform’s economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, of having made racist statements in recent years. Earlier this year, Timothy called Muslims praying in Trafalgar Square an “act of domination”, while Jenrick came under fire in October after the Guardian revealed he had complained he “didn’t see another white face” on a trip to an area of Birmingham.
/politics/2026/oct/17/reform-candidate-f.trail: Exclusive: Bridget Phillipson says politicians have helped fuel hatred and that police are not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough

/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.headline: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.excerpt: NHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases. Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”. The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces.
/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.trail: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use

/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.headline: Trans women no longer to be placed on female-only wards under new NHS England guidance
/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.excerpt: Trans women will no longer be placed on female-only wards under new NHS England guidance on single-sex spaces. The new rules, published on Thursday, mean single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms will be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity. The guidance states that trans people should be “accommodated in line with their biological sex” while ensuring their clinical needs are met and their “privacy, dignity and safety are maintained”, along with other patients sharing their accommodation. It adds that in cases where clinical needs and same-sex accommodation requirements cannot both be met, clinical needs are the priority. Updated guidance for NHS England staff has also been published, stating that all organisations should carry out an audit of their provision to ensure it protects the “privacy, dignity and safety of all staff”. It states that in NHS trusts with mainly single-sex facilities, “suitable and accessible alternatives, such as single‑occupancy or mixed-sex facilities with individual lockable rooms, can be provided”. Previous NHS England guidance said patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity. In a joint statement, TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance said the guidance would “not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges”.
/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.trail: Rules mean single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms will now be used by people based on their biological sex

/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.headline: ‘I get really upset when I visit’: the harsh reality of life in a high-security hospital in England
/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.excerpt: Rampton high-security hospital in Nottinghamshire was built in 1912. Everything about the bleak, remote facility for mentally ill people is forbidding, says Jan Neate. “I get really upset going there,” she says. “Even though I really want to see Jake, visiting is an ordeal.” Jake, 45, is Neate’s son. He has been held at Rampton for eight years. In 2017, many years after being diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, he killed his partner, Suzanne Brown, and was deemed mentally unfit to stand trial. When Neate visits him, her fingerprints and biometrics are taken before she is escorted in. Jake is searched when he is brought into the room and searched again when he leaves. Mother and son are permitted a hug, which is often distressing. “Both of us usually cry when we hug,” says Neate. “It reminds me of what our lives were like before and I think it reminds Jake of that, too.” England has three high-security hospitals – Rampton, Ashworth in Merseyside and Broadmoor in Berkshire. According to the NHS trust that manages Rampton, secure hospitals are for people with severe mental health disorders who pose grave or immediate danger to themselves or to the public. They have accommodated some of the country’s most abhorred criminals, including Peter Sutcliffe, Ronnie Kray, Ian Brady, Ian Huntley and Beverley Allitt. Valdo Calocane, who was convicted of killing three people in 2023 and diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, has spent time in Rampton.
/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.trail: When the Southport killer Axel Rudakubana was transferred from a category A prison to Broadmoor hospital, many observers complained that he was getting off lightly. But as one mother’s story shows, the truth is very different

/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.headline: NHS faces exodus of ADHD and autism services staff to private clinics
/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.excerpt: The NHS is facing an exodus of staff quitting its ADHD and autism services to join private clinics amid huge demand from children and adults to get a diagnosis. The loss of specialist personnel to the private sector has already forced one NHS trust in England to limit access to its neurodevelopmental service to only the most urgent cases. The brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists, nurses and other staff are leaving the NHS “weaker” and making it more likely that people will be forced to seek private healthcare. The NHS care watchdog announced on Friday it will start inspecting private clinics that offer diagnostic assessments for ADHD and autism, which are unregulated. The Care Quality Commission’s move follows the publication of the government-commissioned review of mental health and neurodiversity urging ministers to ensure all service providers are properly regulated amid claims of a “wild west” of private firms offering diagnostic tests. Scores of private clinics have been set up in recent years offering assessments and treatment for ADHD and autism. They have capitalised on the large number of people who have been unable to access NHS care because services have been overwhelmed by an explosion in demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity, creating long waits for help and large backlogs.
/society/2026/oct/17/fifteen-nhs-staff-s.trail: Brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses leaves NHS ‘weaker’, driving patients to seek care elsewhere

/us-news/2026/oct/17/trump-female-cabine.headline: ‘Bold and ethical’: doctors on AOC’s egg-freezing journey - and Maga’s criticisms of it
/us-news/2026/oct/17/trump-female-cabine.excerpt: On Sunday, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced that she is freezing her eggs. The 36-year-old New York congresswoman took to Instagram to document the process, complete with jabbing a syringe into her stomach on camera. “Don’t be weird about this,” Ocasio-Cortez said, “even though I know all of you will be.” As predicted, a cohort of conservative critics emerged on social media to bemoan AOC’s personal choice, which challenges their prescriptive vision for American mothers: young, married and uninterested in pursuing a career. Allie Beth Stuckey, a conservative podcaster and author, is a vocal figure in the proudly antifeminist, pronatalist movement known as the “womanosphere”. She once described herself as “unapologetically pro-life” yet sounded decidedly anti-reproductive health, writing on X that Ocasio-Cortez is “glamorizing the lie that women can have it all. You can’t. Biology is real and how you order your life makes or breaks your future.” Andrew Kolvet, a spokesperson for Turning Point USA, chimed in, writing that egg freezing was “one of the reasons why fertility rates are cratering”. “AOC turns 37 in a few weeks so if she got pregnant tomorrow it would already be a geriatric pregnancy,” added Kolvet, who has no medical credentials.
/us-news/2026/oct/17/trump-female-cabine.trail: In documenting the process, AOC is defying the right’s pronatalist narratives about motherhood and women’s careers

/us-news/2026/oct/17/trump-female-cabine.headline: Judge rules FDA restrictions on mifepristone are arbitrary and capricious
/us-news/2026/oct/17/trump-female-cabine.excerpt: A federal judge upheld the safety of the abortion medication mifepristone and ordered the Trump administration to examine and consider overturning restrictions on the drug as barriers to abortion access mount across the country. Robert S Ballou, a US district judge in Virginia, ordered the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) on Friday to reconsider mifepristone restrictions, which the judge found to be arbitrary and capricious. Previous FDA reviews have “steadfastly found” that mifepristone is safe and effective, Ballou wrote in his decision. Fifth circuit judges are set to hear arguments in a separate case, with Louisiana asking the FDA to reinstate previous restrictions that would block mail-order mifepristone and put limits on pharmacy prescriptions. The FDA, which currently has no permanent commissioner, says it is conducting a review of abortion pill regulations that has been pushed by conservative lawmakers and activists. The case, Whole Woman’s Health Alliance v FDA, was filed in May 2023 by the Center for Reproductive Rights, representing abortion providers in Virginia, Kansas and Montana. “The efforts to restrict it are not about science or safety – they are about making abortion harder to access,” said Nancy Northup, president and CEO at the center, in a statement. She called Friday’s ruling “a win for science”.
/us-news/2026/oct/17/trump-female-cabine.trail: Abortion medication ruled to be safe as judge orders Trump administration to consider overturning restrictions

/world/2026/oct/17/volodymyr-zelenskyy-d.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Russia building non-negotiable ‘security zone’ inside Ukrainian border, Putin declares
/world/2026/oct/17/volodymyr-zelenskyy-d.excerpt: Russia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along the border and it will be non-negotiable in any ⁠future talks with Kyiv, Vladimir Putin has said. The Russian president, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation ⁠was in response to Ukraine’s ⁠2024-25 incursion into Russia’s western Kursk region. “The Russian armed forces were tasked not only with expelling the enemy from our land but also with establishing a security zone ⁠in the adjacent territory. This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments on Friday. “Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions ⁠for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with Ukraine.” The planned ‌security zone spanned 660km (410 ‌miles), of which 70% was currently under Russia’s control, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said. Peskov did not say how deep it would ‌reach inside Ukraine. The zone requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it is illegally claiming as its own territory. Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling the US Congress the pause on the legislation which passed both chambers was in the national interest.
/world/2026/oct/17/volodymyr-zelenskyy-d.trail: Russian president says area will not be part of any potential peace talks while Kremlin puts its size at spanning 660km. What we know on day 1,697

/world/2026/oct/17/volodymyr-zelenskyy-d.headline: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
/world/2026/oct/17/volodymyr-zelenskyy-d.excerpt: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House. Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia. The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump. Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.” Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant. Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.
/world/2026/oct/17/volodymyr-zelenskyy-d.trail: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House

/world/2026/oct/17/volodymyr-zelenskyy-d.headline: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’
/world/2026/oct/17/volodymyr-zelenskyy-d.excerpt: Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire unilaterally declared by Trump on Sunday, having briefly halted its attacks to demonstrate its readiness for peace talks. Russia had continued its strikes on Ukrainian power plants. In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, the US president said: “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace. “There are a lot ‌of targets you can ‌hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, ‌diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.” Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump announced an easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets.
